title: Solvenn Mutual: pricing the safe drivers
prompt: Our client is Solvenn Mutual, a motor insurer with two million policies. For decades it has charged broadly similar premiums to drivers with very different risk. New competitors now use telematics — a phone app that measures how people actually drive — to offer the safest drivers cheaper cover, and Solvenn is losing exactly those customers. Management is considering launching its own usage-based insurance product and has asked us whether it is worth doing.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — Solvenn’s motor book, annual figures
exhibits.unitsNote: The loss ratio is claims as a share of premium; the expense ratio is costs as a share of premium

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — Loss ratio by segment
exhibits.unitsNote: Low-risk: 800K policies. Standard: 1.2M policies. Both pay the same $1,000 average premium today

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — The usage-based product, per low-risk policy
exhibits.unitsNote: Versus today’s $1,000 premium, $550 claims and $250 expenses for the same drivers
exhibits.source: Product team proposal, benchmarked against telematics competitors

rows: One-off cost to build and launch

questions.prompt: Before we evaluate the product, what should we clarify with Solvenn first? Select the two most relevant.
options: How profitable are the customers Solvenn is losing, compared with the ones staying?
What happens to the book if Solvenn does nothing — how many more will leave?
Which celebrity fronts the competitors’ advertising?
What company car does Solvenn’s CFO drive?
How many colours does the claims form come in?

optionRationale: The heart of the case: if the leavers are the profitable ones, this is not ordinary churn but the book being cherry-picked.
The base case. “Launch UBI” is only evaluable against an honest picture of what doing nothing costs.
Advertising talent is not what moves this decision.
Not a data point.
Not a data point.
commonMistakes: Treating all churn as equal instead of asking who exactly is leaving
Evaluating the product against today’s book rather than against the do-nothing trajectory

questions.followUp:
Both questions cut to it. The leavers are Solvenn’s safest drivers — and on the do-nothing path the actuaries expect 300K of the 800K low-risk policies to defect to telematics competitors within a year, with the remainder stable after that.

Here is the book as it stands.

questions.prompt: Which areas would you investigate to decide on the UBI launch? Select the four most relevant.
options: Segment economics — which customers make money today and which lose it
The do-nothing scenario — what the defections cost over the horizon
The UBI product economics — discounted premium, claims effect, and running costs
Risks — regulation on driving data, and discounting customers who would have stayed
The insurer’s branch office refurbishment schedule
The claims department’s softball league results
Historic premium rates from the 1990s

optionRationale: Pricing cases live or die on segmentation; the averages in Exhibit 1 hide the story.
The baseline every option is compared against.
The proposal itself — a discount is only worth giving if the economics behind it hold.
Both named risks are real for telematics pricing and belong in the structure.
Facilities do not bear on a pricing decision.
Not relevant.
Ancient rates say nothing about today’s competitive dynamics.
commonMistakes: Working from book-level averages when the case is about the difference between segments
Forgetting that a discount handed to loyal customers is a cost, not a save

questions.followUp: Let’s size the book first, then split it.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2 splits the book by segment. What does it tell you about Solvenn’s position? Select the two best readings.
options: Low-risk drivers are heavily subsidising the rest of the book at today’s flat pricing
The whole book is unprofitable and should be repriced upward
Competitors are cherry-picking precisely the segment that funds Solvenn’s profitability
Standard drivers should be cancelled immediately
The two segments perform identically

optionRationale: Correct: same premium, 55% versus 80% loss ratio — the safe drivers pay for the risky ones.
Too strong: the book overall runs at a 95% combined ratio, which is profitable.
Correct, and it is why this churn is existential rather than cosmetic: each defection removes a subsidiser.
Repricing or re-selecting standard drivers is a later conversation; cancellation is neither feasible nor implied.
Contradicted by the exhibit.
commonMistakes: Reading the exhibit as a claims problem rather than a cross-subsidy problem
Missing that adverse selection gets worse as each safe driver leaves

questions.followUp: That is the trap of flat pricing: when someone else prices the risk properly, they take your best customers and leave you the rest. Let’s put numbers on the book, then on the segment.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what underwriting profit does the whole motor book make in a year?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Premium: 2.0M × $1,000 = $2.0B.
Claims: 70% = $1,400M. Expenses: 25% = $500M.
Underwriting profit: $2,000M − $1,400M − $500M = $100M a year.
commonMistakes: Applying the ratios to policy count instead of premium
Using only the loss ratio and forgetting expenses

questions.followUp: A $100M profit on a 95% combined ratio — respectable, but thin. Now the segment doing the heavy lifting.

questions.prompt: A low-risk policy today carries a $1,000 premium, $550 of expected claims and $250 of expenses. How much profit does each low-risk policy contribute a year — and what does that imply about the rest of the book?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in dollars per policy, to the nearest dollar.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Per policy: $1,000 − $550 − $250 = $200.
Across 800K low-risk policies that is $160M — more than the whole book’s $100M profit. The standard segment loses money at today’s prices.
commonMistakes: Stopping at the per-policy figure and missing that the segment total exceeds the book total
Using the book-average 70% loss ratio for this segment

questions.followUp:
Exactly: the 800K safest drivers contribute $160M while the book makes $100M — the other 1.2M policies lose $60M between them. Losing 300K of the subsidisers is a $60M-a-year hole.

Here is the product meant to keep them.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, how much profit does a low-risk policy contribute a year on the usage-based product?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in dollars per policy, to the nearest dollar.

commonMistakes: Keeping today’s $550 claims figure — telematics feedback and fairer selection lower it
Forgetting the $20 device and data cost inside the $270
Reading $180 < $200 as “worse” before asking how many policies each scenario keeps

questions.followUp: $180 against $200 today — each retained customer is slightly less profitable, but the point of the product is how many customers there are to retain. Compare the two futures over five years.

questions.prompt: Over five years, how much more profit does launching UBI earn from the low-risk segment than doing nothing? Recall the do-nothing path keeps only 500K of the 800K policies, and the launch costs $50M.
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Do nothing: 500K × $200 = $100M a year → $500M over five years.
UBI: 800K × $180 = $144M a year → $720M, less the $50M build → $670M.
Gain: $670M − $500M = $170M.
commonMistakes: Comparing against today’s 800K book instead of the do-nothing path — the 300K are leaving either way without the product
Forgetting the $50M one-off
Giving the UBI price to only the 300K would-be leavers; in practice the whole segment migrates to the cheaper product

questions.followUp:
A $170M gain over five years, even though every retained customer pays less — volume beats rate here. Note what drives it: $100 of the discount is funded by lower claims, so the margin give-up is small.

Before recommending, the board will want the risks of pricing on driving data.

questions.prompt: What are the most relevant risks of the UBI launch? Select the three most relevant.
options: Cannibalisation — discounting drivers who would have stayed at full price anyway
Data and regulatory risk — collecting driving behaviour raises privacy and fairness questions
Adverse selection worsening in the remaining standard book as flat pricing unravels
Weather risk — more storms meaning more claims
Office relocation risk for the product team

optionRationale: The classic pricing-case risk: the $170M assumes the discount buys retention; for some drivers it just buys down revenue.
Real: telematics pricing runs on personal data, and regulators increasingly ask who is penalised by it.
Real: once safe drivers pay $900, the $1,000 flat price holds only risky drivers — the standard book’s 80% loss ratio drifts worse.
Weather affects both scenarios equally; it is not a UBI risk.
Immaterial.
commonMistakes: Counting every discounted customer as a save
Fixing the low-risk segment and ignoring what the repricing does to the rest of the book

questions.followUp:
Cannibalisation: gate the best discounts behind actual telematics scores rather than giving them on enrolment.

Data: collect the minimum, be transparent about what moves the price, and clear the design with the regulator before launch.

The standard book: this launch is step one of a repricing journey, not the end state — the 80% loss-ratio segment needs its own risk-based pricing next.

questions.prompt: Solvenn’s CEO asks for your recommendation on the usage-based product. Please give your answer in seven to eight lines maximum.

keyPoints: Leads with the recommendation: launch the product
Frames the problem correctly: competitors are cherry-picking the 800K drivers who fund the book’s entire profit
Gives the numbers: $670M versus $500M over five years — a $170M gain after the $50M build
Explains the pricing logic: the 10% discount is mostly funded by a $100 claims reduction, so margin give-up is small
Names the conditions: discounts earned by telematics scores, regulator engaged on data use, and a plan to reprice the standard book next
Stays inside seven or eight lines
commonMistakes: Comparing UBI to today’s book instead of to the do-nothing decline
Presenting the launch as the whole answer when the standard book’s cross-subsidy still needs fixing
Reciting the arithmetic instead of leading with the recommendation

closing: That is the end of the case. Your transcript is ready — copy it into an LLM to be graded on what you actually said, not on what you meant.
